worked_solution.text: As \( x \to 0 \), the numerator \( \sin(2x) - 2x \) tends to \( 0 \).
As \( x \to 0 \), the denominator \( x^{3} + x^{4} \) tends to \( 0 \).

The numerator and the denominator both tend to 0, so the form is \( \frac{0}{0} \) and L'Hospital's rule applies. Differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately: the limit equals \( \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2\cos(2x) - 2}{3x^{2} + 4x^{3}} \).

The new numerator and denominator both tend to 0 again, so the form is still \( \frac{0}{0} \) and the rule applies once more. Differentiate each separately again: the limit equals \( \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-4\sin(2x)}{6x + 12x^{2}} \).

The new numerator and denominator both tend to 0 again, so the form is still \( \frac{0}{0} \) and the rule applies once more. Differentiate each separately again: the limit equals \( \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-8\cos(2x)}{6 + 24x} \).
At \( x = 0 \) this numerator is \( -8 \) and this denominator is \( 6 \), which is not 0, so the limit is \( - \frac{4}{3} \).
